name: Insurance
blurb: Underwriting, claims triage, and fraud detection under active regulator supervision, with NAIC, AM Best, and the Evident insurance index.

reading.body:
The operative constraint on insurance AI is regulatory: the NAIC model bulletin, adopted by a growing majority of states, sets algorithmic-fairness expectations for underwriting, claims triage, and fraud detection.

The pattern is supervision plus external benchmarking. NAIC appears twice, as the source of the model bulletin and as the body setting model-governance expectations, which makes it the binding layer over underwriting AI. AM Best folds innovation and digital maturity into credit opinion, and the Evident AI Index scores insurers on talent, innovation, leadership, and transparency. Together these measure governance and capability, not model output.

The data does not cover compute, data center capacity, or grid constraints, so it cannot support claims about infrastructure limits on insurance AI. It also gives no adoption counts or performance figures beyond the statement that a growing majority of states have adopted the bulletin. What it establishes is that the sector's AI deployments are named and supervised, with fairness expectations attached to the three core use cases.

summary: Underwriting, claims triage, and fraud detection are the deployments regulators are actively supervising.

analysis.body:
The Census Bureau's Business Trends and Outlook Survey, which covers finance and insurance under NAICS 52, found that 41.0% of firms answered yes to using AI in the last two weeks in the latest reading, up from 36.5% in the prior period. The survey first asked the question in September 2023. That is the only measured adoption figure in the material, and it covers the whole finance and insurance sector rather than insurance alone.

The NAIC, the National Association of Insurance Commissioners, describes where the technology sits inside insurance operations. It lists underwriting, pricing, customer service, claims handling, marketing, and fraud detection as the areas where AI is used. Its examples include AI-powered chatbots answering common customer questions and assisting with simple transactions at any time of day, and claims processing tools that estimate repair costs or assess damage from photos and historical data. The NAIC also notes that AI may help insurers move from a detect and repair approach, responding after a loss, to a predict and prevent approach, identifying risks earlier and helping customers avoid losses.

On governance, the NAIC is the operative body. It states that insurers remain responsible for complying with insurance laws, regulations, insurance standards, and consumer protection rules, including requirements on fairness, accuracy, and avoiding unfair discrimination. State insurance regulators oversee insurers' use of AI and may require companies to explain how the tools are used in underwriting, pricing, marketing, or claims decisions, and human oversight remains an important part of insurance decision-making. The NAIC formed the Innovation Cybersecurity and Technology (H) Committee in 2021, formerly the Innovation and Technology (EX) Task Force, and in 2019 established the Big Data and Artificial Intelligence (H) Working Group, which developed regulatory principles on AI adopted by the full NAIC membership at the 2020 Summer National Meeting. Beginning in 2021 the Working Group surveyed insurers by line of business on how AI and machine learning are used and what governance and risk management controls are in place, with aggregate reports on private passenger auto, homeowners, life insurance, and health insurance issued in December 2022, August 2023, December 2023, and May 2025. The NAIC also cautions that large language models do not truly understand context and meaning the way humans do and may generate information that sounds accurate but is incorrect, so AI-generated information should be reviewed carefully, especially for important decisions. It adds that AI is more likely to support human workers than replace them entirely, with actuaries, underwriters, claims professionals, agents, and customer service representatives still reviewing information, exercising judgment, and working directly with consumers.

The Evident AI Index is the sector's comparative maturity scoreboard, benchmarking and tracking AI adoption across financial services. Evident describes itself as an intelligence platform that benchmarks deployment across the sector, spotlights emerging trends, and equips leaders with insights to accelerate AI transformation. It publishes an AI Index for Insurance, with 2026 results, and says the report ranks insurers and profiles leading insurers, showing where the technology is starting to unlock value and where insurers should focus next. Evident also runs an AI Index for Banks and a LATAM edition, and its Banking Brief has over 15,000 subscribers across banking, tech, consulting, academia, and government. Its material notes that several of the world's biggest banks have quietly become AI-powered behemoths and that banks are racing to incorporate the technology into almost everything they do.

AM Best, the insurance rating agency, evaluates innovation and digital maturity as part of its assessments, meaning technology capability reaches credit opinion. The harvested page text for AM Best is limited, so the material supports only that its assessments consider innovation and digital maturity.

For a reader deciding whether to deploy, the material points to a sector where measured use is already substantial and rising, where the use cases are concentrated in underwriting, pricing, customer service, claims handling, marketing, and fraud detection, and where the regulatory posture is active rather than permissive. The NAIC framework expects insurers to explain how AI is used in underwriting, pricing, marketing, or claims decisions, to meet fairness and accuracy requirements, and to keep humans in the decision loop. The NAIC's own caution about LLM errors argues for review of AI-generated output on important decisions. Benchmarking through the Evident AI Index and the rating lens at AM Best suggest that AI capability is being read as a competitive and credit-relevant attribute, not just an internal tooling choice.

https://content.naic.org/.brief: The homepage invites users to explore recent publications, the latest news articles, new federal and legislative news, and model laws. It presents these resources as a way to help inform their approach. The page is organized to provide quick access to up-to-date regulatory information. Users can browse the listed materials to stay current with relevant laws and guidance.

https://content.naic.org/insurance-topic.brief: NAIC created the Innovation Cybersecurity and Technology Committee in 2021 to discuss how new technology, including AI, affects insurance regulation. The Big Data and Artificial Intelligence Working Group, established in 2019, produced regulatory principles on AI that NAIC members adopted in 2020, and has been surveying insurers across lines of business, issuing reports in December 2022, August 2023, December 2023, and May 2025. AI is applied in underwriting, pricing, customer service, claims handling, marketing, and fraud detection, and can help insurers shift from a “detect and repair” approach to a “predict and prevent” strategy. The Working Group notes that while AI can automate many tasks, human oversight remains essential for compliance with fairness, accuracy, and consumer protection rules.
